newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks partially recover from nine-day battering.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks partially recover from nine-day battering.

text.p: Thailand's depressed stock market partially recouped recent losses on Wednesday, climbing back above the key 1,000-point level following a nine-day battering, brokers said.
The index, which finished Tuesday near a three-year low, climbed above the key 1,000-point level briefly before the midday close.
At the break, the index was up 1.71 percent, or 16.75 points, at 998.78.

The market's rise, viewed by some analysts as a technical rebound from recent losses, was assisted by funds from a 15.7 billion baht (US$628 million) private sector rescue fund, which entered the market to help shore up prices, brokers said.
The fund, set up in August and managed by several private fund managers, surprised local participants on Friday in its first major attempt to bolster prices.
"But we are still unsure about the market turnaround and how long this rally will last," said Jongkonnee Wongphasukchot, head of the foreign marketing department at broker Union Securities.
"Most foreign investors appear to be sidelined, although their sales have slowed from earlier sessions."

The rescue fund moved in following heightened speculation that some finance and securities firms, especially smaller ones, may have been hit by defaults by smaller investors unable to top up their stock margin loans, the brokers said.
The rumours, which hit the market on Friday, have forced the stock exchange, several finance firms and the central bank to declare them unfounded.
But despite their denials, speculation has persisted and driven down share prices of local finance firms, traders said.

Signs of weakness in the Thai economy and a no-confidence debate against Thai prime minister Banharn Silpoa-archa set for September 18 have also weighed on the market and caused some anxiety for investors, analysts said.
On Wednesday, the central bank moved again to further dispell fears about the financial health of especially smaller finance firms.
Bank of Thailand spokeswoman Kleo-thong Hetrakul told Reuters the central bank had asked commercial banks to relieve pressure on smaller finance firms by not recalling loans granted to them earlier.
"The (BOT) governor met with commercial banks. During their discussions, he sought cooperation from them to avoid recalling loans granted to small finance firms during this period," she said.

The baht, hit by offshore devaluation rumours from late last week, was weaker on Wednesday but foreign exchange dealers said it was more because of gains posted by the U.S. dollar rather than negative sentiment on the Thai currency.
"The baht continued to fall against the dollar as the U.S. unit is rising abroad. There was nothing involving the rumour against the baht," said one currency dealer.
The baht was trading lower at 25.372-25.375 to the dollar in midday activity against 25.354-25.359 late on Tuesday.
The midrate at which the baht was fixed by the central bank on Wednesday was at an eight-week low.
